Week 8 question: In August, Police Chief Shavies gave a presentation to the City Council on the issues he’s seeing with e-bikes in the community. He was concerned about the lack of education around purchasing e-bikes and, in turn, the increased injury risk to younger riders if they’ve purchased an e-bike far more powerful than expected. What is your personal experience with e-bikes and your perspective on whether the city should regulate e-bikes in addition to what the state does? Adam Hundt (http://adamhundt.com/) Certainly, Piedmont must prioritize resident and rider safety. As e-bikes are more widely adopted, hospitals are noting an increase in injuries due to these devices. I believe a first step to ensure safe e-bike riding in Piedmont is to educate residents on this issue. If warranted by data from the Piedmont Police Department, it is reasonable to explore creating a local ordinance regarding e-bikes. Currently, there is a lack of awareness about California rules regarding e-bikes. Certain bikes are in fact, electric motorcycles capable of speeds over 20 mph and should not be used by teenagers unless they have a motorcycle license. Riders under age 18 must use a helmet on an e-bike. E-bikes must have proper lighting or a reflector. I agree with Police Chief Shavies, who said in an August 2026 presentation to Piedmont City Council, “Our goal is education before enforcement.” City government can work with Piedmont Police to provide education through Piedmont schools, parent groups, and community events, while also gathering data on e-bike incidents in the city. As needed, Piedmont could explore steps such as the ordinance passed in Danville, which requires e-bike riders to walk devices in park spaces and limits speeds on trails. articles.text: Editor: I want to thank the Board of Education for their service and for adoption of the new AGA math curriculum. However, I’m writing to express my frustration with the Board’s adoption of the new Math “Don’t-call-it-compression-for-all” Pathways despite the impassioned testimony from the PMS and PHS math teachers, who spent nearly four hours Wednesday evening at the Board meeting in protest of the new policy and the process by which it was arrived at. The Board is rightfully concerned about the roughly 30% of PMS students who perform below state math standards. Ariel Dolowich presented clear data showing that the majority of these students are in the grade-level track, which essentially only demonstrates that district staff is categorizing the performance of the children correctly. Not presented was any data or research showing that eliminating the grade-level track and putting these lower performing students in a track designed to prepare them for Algebra I in 8th grade would be efficacious. Nor was any evidence presented on the effects this may have on the higher performing students. Mr. Dolowich took issue with the October 14th Post’s characterization of the new single track as “Compression for all,” but failed to clarify if this is then “grade level math for all” or how you can have all students prepared for Algebra in 8th grade without “compression.” Put simply, are we raising the bar or lowering it? Would raising the bar help struggling students? Would lowering the bar still engage our high performers? Should we perhaps instead keep two parallel bars with some pathways to jump between them, or even increase the number of bars with more fluid groupings of students on a yearly or semester basis? The Board’s public comments on this lack of evidence essentially boiled down to “we have to do something” and “we are small so we can be nimble.” How do the parents and teaching professionals feel about the experiment the Board is running on our middle schoolers? I am hoping my 6th grader continues to thrive in Mr. Barile-Hill’s math class and that the experiment will play itself out before my TK’er reaches 6th grade.
articles.title: Math detracking at PMS?

articles.text: Editor: I am Michael Henn, a longtime Piedmont resident, former Piedmont Planning Commissioner, and three-time member of the Alameda County Civil Grand Jury. The nonpartisan and independent Civil Grand Jury Association, not affiliated with the sitting Grand Jury, evaluates local ballot measures’ language for fairness and accuracy. There are eight measures evaluated in the attached report, including one from Piedmont. By chance, Piedmont’s Measure H achieved the highest score of the eight. As reported, local ballot measures unfairly exaggerate the measures’ benefits while ignoring the costs. Local ballot measure ratings for Alameda County General Election on Nov. 3 Created by independent Civil Grand Jury Association The 29 Alameda County local ballot measures scheduled for the November 3, 2026 general election were evaluated in September 2026 by the Alameda County Ballot Watchdog Committee. The measures’ titles were evaluated for the accuracy and fairness required by the California Elections Code using criteria established by the committee for each type of ballot measure, e.g., Bond Measure, Tax Measure, and Other (non-tax measure). This article will review Measure GG and Measure RTM. The collective scores represent the average score arrived at by the evaluators who have served on previous civil grand juries (up to 15 evaluators allowed). The scoring system is comparable to the popular “Yelp” type scoring system (a score of one is worst; five is best). Like a Yelp evaluation, the ratings reflect the average of the evaluators’ educated opinions, based on the established criteria as to what should be, and should not be, included in each type of ballot measure. The Ballot Watchdog group IS NOT evaluating the merits of the measures. The evaluation is non-partisan, neither liberal nor conservative. They are only concerned with the accuracy and impartiality of the up-to-75-word ballot title being presented to the voters. State law requires ballot language to be “a true and impartial synopsis of the purpose of the proposed measure and shall be in language that is neither argumentative nor likely to create prejudice for or against the measure.” Unfortunately, local jurisdictions violate the law’s intent by exaggerating benefits, glossing over costs, and adding extraneous verbiage designed to favor passage of the measure. It’s easy to understand the cause of this bias: No one, other than the agency promoting the measure’s passage, is required to approve the agency’s language. To counteract this inherent bias, we need active, consistent monitoring of local government ballot language, aka “Ballot Titles.” This current Ballot Watchdog Committee effort implements the findings of the 2021 Alameda County Civil Grand Jury Report, The Need for Accuracy and Impartiality of Ballot Measure Questions. Additional information on the 2021 report and all other Alameda County Civil Grand Jury Reports is available on the Alameda County website: https:// grandjury.acgov.org. Information on the work of the Alameda County Ballot Watchdog Committee is at ballotwatchdog.com. Results: The Ballot Watchdog Committee’s review produced individual ballot measure scores ranging from 1.8 to 4.6. The average was 3.71. The most common matter that caused a reduction in the score was a lack of clarity as to why the measure was needed and what it would cost. Almost as common was the inclusion of extraneous verbiage designed to influence a favorable vote on the measure. Numerous proposed tax increases failed to mention that the new tax is being added to an existing similar tax and what that existing tax is, and what the resulting tax will be. articles.text: Editor: I strongly encourage those reading this to vote yes on Measure GG. I previously spent six years on Piedmont’s Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee, including two years as Chair. During that time period, the Committee consistently pointed out the City is facing increasing costs due to inflation and growing need for infrastructure maintenance and capital investment to maintain the level of services that Piedmont residents expect. Given that the City is primarily reliant on property-related tax revenue, and as the Committee pointed out in prior reports, increasing the Transfer Tax as proposed in Measure GG is “the most broadbased and sustainable source for material additional revenue.” Please join me in supporting Measure GG. –Frank Ryan
articles.title: Yes on Measure GG

articles.text: Editor: I’m a progressive who believes in government and in paying taxes to support public services. I’m voting No on Measure GG, and I hope you’ll join me in sending it back to the City Council for a better version. I strongly support raising revenue for city services and parks and recreation. As others have pointed out, they’re a big reason my family chose Piedmont. But GG is the wrong tool for three main reasons. First, it’s an unreliable revenue source that will hurt homeowners. Studies of transfer taxes in Toronto, New York, and Germany find they reduce the number of home sales and lower prices. Fewer sales means less revenue for the city, but Piedmont needs a sustainable and consistent revenue source. Second, it’s unclear how the money will be spent. GG is a general tax with no dedicated uses and no reporting requirement. Supporters have said it will pay for parks, public safety, and city employee benefits. It can’t fund everything mentioned, and voters will have no way to hold the city accountable for how GG funds are spent. Third, it’s a band-aid. Piedmont’s budget squeeze comes from having almost no commercial tax base and from Prop 13, which prevents property tax revenue from keeping pace with home values and the real cost of running a city. Prop 13 already makes our revenue depend on who happens to sell, and GG doubles down on that instead of spreading the burden among all homeowners. Not having a commercial tax base is a choice and one we can also fix. Vote No, and ask the Council to come back with a measure that provides dependable revenue, has dedicated uses, and spreads the costs fairly among all homeowners. I’ll vote for that one. –Erin Yaylali
articles.title: Vote No on Measure GG

articles.text: Editor: My family and I live on a busy arterial street and a crosswalk used to terminate in our driveway. Five years ago, our street was identified in Piedmont’s Safer Streets Plan as a location where pedestrian and vehicle safety could be improved. About two years ago, funding became available to make these significant improvements in our neighborhood possible. These changes have made our street so much safer now for pedestrians and cars alike. They were not done in isolation; the City is implementing pedestrian and road safety projects around Piedmont. We support Measure GG in the hope that the generated revenue can keep our essential services strong and continue to address other important traffic and pedestrian safety projects around town. We encourage others to support Measure GG. –Amy and Tom McKenzie

articles.text: Editor: As a Piedmont resident for over 50 years, I value our community and the things that make it a good place to live. The adage is that people come to Piedmont for the schools and stay for the public services. I’ve been lucky enough to experience both. As a teacher and principal in our schools, I got to help our children grow and learn. As a community member, I’ve taken advantage of the recreation, public safety, and other services our tax dollars provide. Measure GG will help the city catch up with the increasing expenses it faces every day. It proposes a modest increase in a tax only paid when properties are sold. The measure will provide additional revenue, allocated annually and in public, to maintain our essential public services and facilities and to continue the high level of service we expect from our city government. Local ballot measure ratings for Alameda County General Election on Nov. 3 Created by independent Civil Grand Jury Association The 29 Alameda County local ballot measures scheduled for the November 3, 2026 general election were evaluated in September 2026 by the Alameda County Ballot Watchdog Committee. The measures’ titles were evaluated for the accuracy and fairness required by the California Elections Code using criteria established by the committee for each type of ballot measure, e.g., Bond Measure, Tax Measure, and Other (non-tax measure). This article will review Measure GG and Measure RTM. The collective scores represent the average score arrived at by the evaluators who have served on previous civil grand juries (up to 15 evaluators allowed). The scoring system is comparable to the popular “Yelp” type scoring system (a score of one is worst; five is best). Like a Yelp evaluation, the ratings reflect the average of the evaluators’ educated opinions, based on the established criteria as to what should be, and should not be, included in each type of ballot measure. They are only concerned with the accuracy and impartiality of the up-to-75-word ballot title being presented to the voters. State law requires ballot language to be “a true and impartial synopsis of the purpose of the proposed measure and shall be in language that is neither argumentative nor likely to create prejudice for or against the measure.” Unfortunately, local jurisdictions violate the law’s intent by exaggerating benefits, glossing over costs, and adding extraneous verbiage designed to favor passage of the measure. It’s easy to understand the cause of this bias: No one, other than the agency promoting the measure’s passage, is required to approve the agency’s language. The most common matter that caused a reduction in the score was a lack of clarity as to why the measure was needed and what it would cost. Almost as common was the inclusion of extraneous verbiage designed to influence a favorable vote on the measure. Numerous proposed tax increases failed to mention that the new tax is being added to an existing similar tax and what that existing tax is, and what the resulting tax will be. articles.text: In November, Piedmont residents will vote to fill three seats on the City Council. Among the candidates running for City Council is Adam Hundt, a Bay Area resident for 20 years who moved to Piedmont in 2021 with his wife and two young children. Hundt has a 14-year career in the technology industry, primarily in e-commerce, and now works in the energy and climate sector, most recently on a California wildfire risk mitigation project. Hundt grew up in Maryland and holds an MBA and masters degree in industrial engineering from the University of Michigan and a public policy degree from Johns Hopkins University. His first job in tech was working for eBay in the mid-2000s. He learned that well-designed platforms and incentives can help people transact and create value for both sides. “eBay was a company that was doing well by doing good by creating opportunities for small business entrepreneurs to be successful merchants on their marketplace platform, and so that was appealing to me from a values perspective,” said Hundt. Hundt transitioned away from the tech industry into public policy because he wanted to help build a better world. “My interest in government comes from my youth, growing up around the federal government and my desire in my professional life to take roles that would make a positive impact on people’s lives,” said Hundt. Hundt believes we have the technology to lower carbon emissions and build a better environment. But the biggest obstacle is getting businesses to adopt these changes. This is a problem he feels adequately equipped to solve. “It feels like I can use my business skills to help solve that type of problem. I found from my business life that if there’s a clear financial incentive to do something, it becomes a huge motivator for someone to act and adopt a service or a product,” said Hundt. Hundt’s passion for public policy inspired him to run for Piedmont’s City Council. He was attracted to the position after experiencing the strong sense of community in Piedmont and his desire to make a positive impact in the area where he now resides. Adam Hundt “We’re making a home here in Piedmont. This is an opportunity to have a positive impact on our children’s lives, as well as the lives of all the residents. That’s a very exciting opportunity that I would love to be a part of,” said Hundt. Hundt likes to spend time with his wife and children and describes himself as a film aficionado. Hundt is is a member of the SF Film and the Berkeley Pacific Film Archive, where he’ll watch an old classic if he has the time. When asked for his top three movies, he responded with The Princess Bride, Big starring Tom Hanks, and Say Anything.

articles.text: Nancy Beninati is running for one of the three open seats on Piedmont’s City Council. Beninati grew up in New York, went to Cornell University, and went to law school at the Golden Gate University School of Law. She has two kids attending Piedmont High School and has been married for over 20 years. Beninati began her legal career in Walnut Creek representing the families of people who had died in the Oakland Hills fire. Since then, she’s dedicated her legal career to helping people “I’ve taken my professional career on a trajectory of helping people. I’ve spent over 20 years focused on civil rights and civil rights enforcement,” said Beninati. Beninati served 27 years at the California Department of Justice as a Supervising Deputy Attorney General and now teaches law and public policy at the Goldman School of Public Policy. She has held multiple leadership roles with the League of Women Voters Piedmont, including serving two terms as its President. She currently serves on the Piedmont Recreation Commission and previously served as Chair of the Piedmont Civil Service Commission. One of her accomplishments she’s most proud of in her legal career is her work on racial profiling. Beninati led a Racial and Identity Profiling Advisory Board that collected data from over 500 police departments in California on this issue. The board relesed annual reports and worked with police departments on reform efforts. “It’s helped in a lot of the police reform work that I did. We used the racial and identity profiling data and information that we got to inform our reforms in cities like San Francisco and Bakersfield,” said Beninati. Beninati plans to scale back from her work at the California Department of Justice to focus on her teaching. With this extra time, she decided to run for Piedmont City Council to continue working in public policy and serve the community. “I love public policy and being involved in community service. I think it’s a good time for me to run for council. I really value listening to the community, and I have the government and public Nancy Beninati policy experience,” said Beninati. She values Piedmont’s community engagement and the accessibility of city employees to talk about the decisions the city makes. “I appreciate being able to walk down to town hall and talk to the building planner directly, where I know that that’s not necessarily a situation in other larger cities,” said Beninati. After the election is over, Beninati plans to participate in the Wednesday Walkers tours to see the history of the city and learn more about her family’s history in Piedmont.
articles.title: Profile: City Council candidate Nancy Beninati

articles.text: The Piedmont Boosters Club is hosting its largest fundraising event, Oktoberfest, this Saturday, October 24. The Club relies on these community fundraiser events to support high school athletics. The event will feature a beer garden with local craft breweries and a premium wineand-spritz station, held at the Community Hall from 4 to 9 p.m. The Athletics Boosters Club was founded in 1978 to help Piedmont’s school athletic programs. According to the Boosters Club’s website, over 78% of Piedmont High School students participate in athletics across 48 teams and 17 sports. The school district provides essentials such as uniforms, field and practice space, and protective equipment; anything further relies on outside sources of “We come in where the district can’t,” said Boosters Club President Keri Elmquist. “Beyond the basic supplies, it falls on us to help supply the teams for our student athletes. We stepped in as In her sixth year as president, Elmquist has witnessed the positive effects of supporting youth “My three kids all came through Piedmont in various sports, and it was probably the highlight of all of their high school careers,” Elmquist continued. “There’s nothing like playing for your team in your town, A group having fun at the 2025 Oktoberfest. in front of your friends and your families. To the extent we can just get behind that in any and every way possible, that’s our mission.” To support these athletes, the Club contributes to the teams through grant distributions. Each team has a liaison to represent it. The team captains and coaches can approach these liaisons with a grant request. The coach and liaison will write an explanation of what they need and where they’d source it. The executive committee and board do an initial evaluation of the request before voting on it at their monthly meeting. These requests typically pertain to improving individual teams’ equipment, athletic departments, facilities, and, in some cases, capital improvements. Elmquist gave an example of what they fund. The lacrosse team requested practice sticks to help new kids in the program who had never played before and did not have their own equipment. To fund these grant requests, the Club hosts fundraisers and paid memberships to support the programs. Oktoberfest is the Club’s biggest event, and they expect to raise about $50,000 for the Boosters Club through ticket sales and sponsorships. Athletes will volunteer to prepare and serve food to guests. General admission provides five pours of beer or wine, one sausage, and one pretzel. Ticket packages can be purchased online at https://www.piedmontoktoberfest.com/. The Piedmont Athletics Boosters Club is a nonprofit organization that supports athletics at Piedmont High School and the middle schools.

One of the greater mysteries of our cosmos is dark matter. Unlike regular matter, which can easily be perceived, dark matter is an invisible substance. By unlocking the mysteries of dark matter, scientists learn more about our universe. A Mysterious Discovery Dark matter has been an ongoing mystery for scientists for decades. It wasn’t until the 1970s that the existence of dark matter was accepted by the scientific community. While observing spiral galaxies, astronomer Vera Rubin noted that there must be something keeping the stars on the outer edge of the spiral from flying out into space. Based on her observations, Rubin concluded that the invisible glue keeping the stars in place must be dark matter. Although there is still debate from scientists on what exactly dark matter could be, its general existence is widely agreed upon. It is known that dark matter has gravity and that it doesn’t emit, reflect, absorb, or even block light; it simply passes through normal matter just like a ghost. Although dark matter doesn’t interact with light, scientists have observed that its gravity can cause light from distant galaxies to bend, an effect scientists have called gravitational lensing. ing, scientists can better understand dark matter and its effects on the universe. articles.text: From explaining concepts to generating entire assignments, artificial intelligence is changing how Generation Z students approach school work. By offering instant explanations and assistance on assignments, AI appeals to students, however this generation maintains a healthy fear of the dangers its capabilities hold. At Piedmont High School (PHS), students use AI platforms like ChatGPT, Claude, and Google Gemini to help them study for tests, and refresh material on topics that they aren’t as confident in, junior Izara Dando said. “I think it’s a helpful resource for understanding concepts and it provides me with practice tests that are efficient,” Dando said. The curriculum at PHS moves quickly, especially in advanced courses. Junior Quinn Wagener said she uses AI to go over material she didn’t fully understand during class. “It helps me learn better when I can fully grasp the main ideas of the concept,” Wagener said. “When I am stuck on a concept, I can ask it to explain it to me.” Although AI is commonly viewed as a helpful resource, students acknowledge the dangers of using platforms excessively. “The more students use AI consistently, the more we rely on it for assignments,” Wagener said. “This could negatively affect how we comprehend ideas with no AI use.” As Gen Z becomes further dependent on AI, it is beginning to affect the way people think and operate on a daily basis, junior Noah Baldwin said. “AI is further reinforcing the loss of creativity,” Baldwin said. “It is causing growing minds to become people with limited imaginations.” To ensure that they don’t become dependent, students are focusing on the importance of limiting their AI use. Dando said she acknowledges the dangers AI holds in the future and takes that into consideration in her everyday life. “In the future it might make people less critical and take away opportunities of occupations,” Dando said. The dangers of AI use largely depend on the user themselves, and the extent that they rely on the platform, Dando said. “Some people may misuse AI and grow to depend on it, but for others I think it can be beneficial,” Dando said Over the past few years, students have seen an increase in the use of AI, because of its ability to provide support and help for assignments and everyday tasks, Wagener said. “It has increased but not by much. I think as my workload increases I use it more because I get more drained and can’t fully comprehend what I am learning,” Wagener said. At Piedmont High School, the AI Overview Google page has been blocked on all school-issued Chromebooks. This new restriction has made it more difficult for students to access AI when looking up topics or questions, Dando said. “It’s difficult because no matter what you look up, you have to scroll through various links to find the answer you are searching for, which you may never find,” Dando said. When it comes to AI usage, current students must balance the need for speedy answers with the desire to fight off technology dependence. How much AI aid each student needs can correlate to looming deadlines and heavy courseloads, making time management and structure increasingly important. Ayla Blanford is a Piedmont High School junior and a student writer intern for the Piedmont Post.

See details below: • 6th grade: Nearly all students take the same rigorous 6th grade math curriculum, with extra support available. • 7th grade: Students take Pre-Algebra I, with extra support as needed. This is the one year that will cover more content. • 8th grade: A growing number of students will continue to Algebra I. Students who need or want more time will take Pre-Algebra II followed by Algebra I in 9th grade. Readiness will be the primary consideration. Pre-Algebra I combines 7th grade standards with some 8th grade standards and strategic built-in support will be provided. Placement in Pre-Algebra II or Algebra will strictly follow readiness. Piedmont High’s boys’ water polo team gained a 15-8 win over Lick-Wilmerding in San Francisco on Tuesday, October 13. The result improved their record to 10-10 overall and 3-2 against Western Alameda County Conference opponents with one Henry Stein scored seven goals in Piedmont’s win over Lick-Wilmerding. match left in the regular season. It was a strong offensive day for Piedmont’s two leading scorers, Henry Stein and Rylan Patty, with seven and five goals respectively. The Highlanders played their final regular season game yesterday, October 20, against rival Bishop O’Dowd. With a victory, they will end the season as the WACC’s second-ranked team. They now prepare for the first round of the WACC Tournament on Tuesday, October 27 at Encinal, with the second round on October 29, and finals on Halloween, October 31. Match Recap Piedmont led 3-2 through the first quarter and dominated the second quarter to lead 8-4 by halftime. PHS maintained a fourgoal lead through the third quarter, 11-7, adding four more goals in the fourth quarter while only conceding one. In the first, nearly half of the quarter played without a goal until Lick struck first at the 3:46 mark. 50 seconds later, PHS drew a five-meter penalty, leading to Rylan Patty launching in a goal to tie the game. However, the Tigers regained the lead just 11 seconds later on its next possession. It took just 12 seconds for Piedmont to tie it up, once again, at 2:32 when Henry Stein scored. Graham Smith gave PHS the lead with 29 seconds remaining in the first. Lick tied the match at 3-3 just 19 seconds into the second quarter at 6:41, but that’s the closest things would get from then on. The Highlanders drew another five-meter penalty at the 5:22 mark, leading to Stein scoring his second goal. PHS added two more goals by Patty and Stein to lead 6-3 with 3:41 left. Lick scored its fourth at 2:04, leading to two more unanswered goals by Stein to give his team an 8-4 lead with 34 seconds left before halftime.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ tennis team split its last two Western Alameda County Conference matches over the past week. They recently swept Berkeley 7-0 at the Berkeley Tennis Club on Thursday, October 15, but lost 4-3 to Alameda the previous day at the Corey Reich Tennis Center. The results brings Piedmont’s record to 11-5 overall. Te loss to Alameda is their only league defeat at 4-1, putting them behind the Hornets as the regular season winds to a close. PHS will get one more shot at Alameda in the season-finale next week on October 28. A win will mean they can share the WACC title. “It was really close against Alameda and we had our chances. We look forward to our second match against them, I’m sure it will be another great match,” coach Jim Landes said. Junior Leela Sivakumar had a successful pair of matches against Alameda and Berkeley. She beat Alameda’s Natalie Gilbert in straight sets, which avenges two consecutive losses she had to Gilbert. “Against Alameda, I actually played this girl four times and lost the last two. I was determined going in, and I played a lot over the weekend and did a lot of footwork drills. Being able to be consistent, move my feet, and get to the ball to the right spot is what helped me get there. She has an interesting playing style that threw me off the last times I played her, so I knew she was consistent and switch things up from a huge forehand to a soft slice,” Sivakumar said. 7-0 over Berkeley Piedmont made quick work of the Yellowjackets in its one-sided sweep. Emma Chan and Chiara Silvio started the day with a 6-0, 6-1 win at No. 1 doubles, and was quickly followed by Maddy Huynh winning 6-0, 6-0 at No. 3 singles. From there, Faith Chin also won by a shutout score of 6-0, 6-0 at No. 2 singles. Clinching the match day was Ella Ruthven at No. 1 singles, winning 6-3, 6-0. articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont goes into their league tournament with a 9-10 overall record and 8-6 league record, meaning they have clinched the team’s first NCS birth in school history. Piedmont High’s flag football team suffered a 31-6 loss to Bishop O’Dowd on Thursday, October 15 at Witter Field for its regular season finale. It brings their record to 9-10 overall and 8-6 against Western Alameda County Conference teams as they enter the league tournament. Piedmont held a 6-6 tie through much of the first half, but the Dragons finished the game with 25 unanswered points, including 19 of them in the second half. The game provides a lesson in finishing for the Highlanders after allowing a touchdown on the final play of the first half, while the Highlanders’ offense had multiple drives end on O’Dowd’s side of the field. “We might see O’Dowd next Thursday [in the WACC Tournament]. Now they’ve seen how they play and know how to react. The attitude has coalesced, and there’s a unified drive to them. The lesson is it’s not all the defense’s job, the offense has to finish. They have the drive to do it, but there’s the follow and the finish. They have the follow, now we have to finish,” coach Beth Black said. Regardless of the result, Piedmont’s league record going into the WACC Tournament means they have automatically clinched a spot in the North Coast Section playoffs for the first time. “The next week is now lined up for them. It’s a first, and that’s something very special for this group,” Black said. Piedmont honored its 11 seniors on the roster, including Kaylani Despanie, Jo Palsa, Ellie Olsen, Naiya Alexander, Anjali Bowers, Brynne Jones, Kate Tong, Agatha Filha Gama, Bea Nackley, Skye Prata Baack, and Carmela DiLauro. For Tong, she is a two-year member of the varsity squad, watching them improve from 5-13 last season to achieve the school’s first-ever NCS berth. “It’s super exciting, it’s another week or two playing flag football. It’s my senior year, so I’m taking advantage of all the time I can get. It’s special to qualify and we deserve it. I’m really proud how we’ve played,” Tong said. Game Recap Both teams went scoreless through the first quarter, including Piedmont’s defense forcing two turnovers on downs. articles.text: Mt. Tamalpais has well over 100 miles of trails to hike; from the steep and strenuous, to the relaxed and nature focused. For this venture, we walk 1.5 miles on the Dawn Falls Trail to the Southern Marin Line Fire Road until reaching the Barbara Springs Trail and back to the car, making an easy but stunning 3.5 mile hike. Its Dawn Falls Trail is a short and popular 1.4 mile walk with over 510 feet in elevation gain to its main attraction, Dawn Falls. Although the “Falls” is more of a trickle given its only active during or after a heavy rain, the walk shows you what makes Mt. Tam so magnificent. At times, you will pass through narrow corridors of redwood trees that look something out of a fairytale with steam raising off it during the morning hours. Starting at the Dawn Falls Trailhead on Madrone Avenue in Larkspur, the trail along the inactive Larkspur Creek is a palette of vibrant fall colors from maple leaves; redwoods tower over in every direction, while lush green moss covers every tree, stone, and branch. It is worth mentioning that Staff Photos A narrow corridor of redwood trees is shown along the Dawn Falls Trail on Mt. Tamalpais. the Dawn Falls Trail is a mostly slim passage of under three-feet wide—meaning you will have to be patient when passing by hikers, runners, and an inevitable number of groups during weekends. Our 10 a.m. walk up to the falls passed a staggering 49 people in the 1.5 miles, passing another 34 people in the remaining two miles back to the car— making 83 people passed in total, so near 24 other patrons per mile. For those conscious of personal space, continue on the Southern Marin Line Fire Road; a dirt road which is wide enough to adequate two lanes of cars. Otherwise, you can continue up the Hoo Koo E Koo Trail and Blithedale Ridge trails, which will more than double your elevation gain to provide a workout of near 1,200 feet until re-intersecting with the fire road. You’ll get glimpses of Mt. Tam’s eastern peak from the fire road. The 0.5 mile walk down the Barbara Springs Trail back to the car is a very steep 500-foot descent with tree roots , n every direction, so be wary. articles.text: The Piedmont Avenue Halloween Parade was started in 1987 by a number of Piedmont Avenue merchants who “wanted to give kids a safe place to trick-or-treat,” recalled the late Richard Stone, owner of Continental Hearing. articles.text: An exhibition at the Legion of Honor in San Francisco explores how photographers helped shape the image of Paris through photographs documenting the city’s architecture, cultural heritage and transformation into a modern metropolis. Eternal Paris: Photographing the City of Light is on view now, featuring nearly 50 photographs from the Achenbach Foundation for Graphic Arts, many of which have never been exhibited publicly. The exhibition traces the work of photographers in the 19th and early 20th centuries who documented Paris’ historic landmarks, preserved its architectural heritage and captured the changes that reshaped the city. Their images helped establish Paris as an international center of art and culture. Among the works are early photographs of the city’s celebrated monuments, images of the ruins left by the Paris Commune of 1871 and photographs documenting Paris as it stood on the threshold of modernity. The exhibition also features works by photographers including Édouard-Denis Baldus, Eugène Atget and Brassaï. Atget is known for his extensive photographic documentation of Paris, recording its streets, buildings and neighborhoods during a period of significant urban change. Together, the photographs show how the medium helped preserve the city’s past while documenting its evolution. They also reveal how photographers contributed to the romanticized image of Paris that continues to influence how the city is viewed today. Eternal Paris: Photographing the City of Light is on view at the Legion of Honor, 100 34th Ave. in San Francisco, through February 28, 2027. For information, visit famsf. org/exhibitions/eternal-parisphotographing-city-light. articles.text: Oakland Ballet Company performs Luna Mexicana, a ballet celebrating Día de los Muertos and traditional Mexican dance, on October 30 and November 1 at the Paramount Theatre in Oakland. Luna Mexicana is an original work by Oakland Ballet Company’s Artistic Director Graham Lustig and is one of the Bay Area’s most celebrated events honoring Día de los Muertos, or Day of the Dead, a holiday celebrated and observed mostly in Mexico and Latin America. Lustig’s production features a young woman whose ancestors “dance” back to life in the form of teetering skeletons, skirt-swishing ladies and a bride and groom duet. In 2018, Oakland Ballet Company premiered Viva la Vida, co-choreographed by Lustig and Martín Romero of Ballet Folklorico Mexico Danza. The dance celebrates the life and artistry of iconic Mexican artist Frida Kahlo, and is now included in annual presentations of Luna Mexicana. Past performances have included the Aztec ensemble Nahui-Ehekatl and Co. and dancers from Ballet Folklorico Mexico Danza . Audience members of all ages are encouraged to attend in Day of the Dead costume. Luna Mexicana is a family-friendly event and ideal for audience members ages 7 and up. articles.text: Opera performed Oct. 31 through Nov. 29 San Francisco Opera will present Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart’s The Marriage of Figaro October 31 through November 29 at the War Memorial Opera House. The production, directed by the late Michael Cavanagh, returns to the company following its 2019 debut. Shawna Lucey directs the revival, and conductor Sebastian Weigle makes his San Francisco Opera debut leading the orchestra and cast. The opera premiered in Vienna in 1786 and was the first of three collaborations between Mozart and librettist Lorenzo Da Ponte, followed by Don Giovanni in 1787 and Così fan tutte in 1790. Based on a French play by Pierre Beaumarchais, the comic opera explores class divisions through the story of Figaro and Susanna as they prepare to marry. Cavanagh’s production sets the story in an American manor house during Mozart’s time. It was the first installment of San Francisco Opera’s planned Mozart-Da Ponte trilogy. Slovak bass Peter Kellner makes his company debut in the title role, with Slovak soprano Slávka Zámečníková as Susanna. The cast also includes Canadian soprano Olivia Smith as Countess Almaviva, mezzo-soprano Simone McIntosh as Cherubino and British baritone Thomas Mole as Count Almaviva. The opera will be performed in Italian with English supertitles. Conductor Sebastian Weigle San Francisco Opera dramaturg emeritus Clifford “Kip” Cranna will give a 20-minute pre-opera talk 55 minutes before each performance. The November 7 performance at 7:30 p.m. will be livestreamed, with on-demand viewing available for 48 hours beginning November 8 at 10 a.m. Livestream tickets cost $25. Performances are scheduled for Oct. 31; Nov. 3, 7, 10, 13, 15, 18, 21, 27 and 29. Evening performances begin at 7:30 p.m., and matinees begin at 2 p.m. The War Memorial Opera House is at 301 Van Ness Ave. in San Francisco. For tickets and information, call the box office at (415) 864-3330 or visit sfopera. com.

articles.text: Scene from Peter Pan Goes Wrong San Francisco Playhouse is presenting Peter Pan Goes Wrong, a comedy about an amateur theater company attempting to stage Peter Pan while a series of mishaps threatens to derail the production. Written by Henry Lewis, Henry Shields and Jonathan Sayer, the play follows the fictional Cornley Polytechnic Drama Society as its members take on J.M. Barrie’s classic story. The production features flying rigs, sword fights and a crocodile, along with forgotten lines, malfunctioning scenery and rivalries that spill onto the stage. The play is by the creators of The Play That Goes Wrong, which similarly follows a fictional theater troupe whose production goes increasingly awry. Peter Pan Goes Wrong premiered in London in 2013 before later moving to the West End and Broadway. Susi Damilano directs the San Francisco production. articles.text: Shotgun Players presents a surreal romance story of older love based on the works of playwright Charles Mee, directed and choreographed by Erika Chong Shuch. The Fall Show features main characters Eddie and Sam, who are joined by a six-person ensemble that serves to disrupt and evoke the ups and downs of falling in love. Mee was an American playwright, historian and author known for experimental plays that combined classical literature, historical texts, popular culture and contemporary themes. His best-known plays include Big Love, a contemporary adaptation of the Greek tragedy The Suppliants; bobrauschenbergamerica, inspired by the collage art of Robert Rauschenberg; Orestes 2.0 and The Trojan Women: A Love Story, modern adaptations of Greek tragedies; and Hotel Cassiopeia, about artist Joseph Cornell. In a press release, director Shuch said she and dramaturg Sarah Rose Leonard “combed the expanse of Charles Mee’s corpus of plays for a story that resonated.” “I’ve been thinking about how the love stories of middle-aged and older adults—and I include myself in this category—are muted. Falling in love, being in love, maintaining love: it’s complicated, twisty, chaotic,” said Shuch. “I hope I continue to be baffled by how to love, because it means I’m still thinking about it, still trying for it, still rooting for it, still valuing it.” Tickets are available for purchase at www.shotgunplayers. org/show/fall/ or by calling the box office: 510-841-6500 x 303. articles.text: It’s good to be home. While we were in Europe, we had the opportunity to hear a number of concerts. And then as soon as we returned, we heard concerts in this area. Comparing the philosophy of these concerts presents profound thoughts. First and foremost, concerts are entertainment. A few things come to mind. The repertoire must be as well thought out as an excellent meal is presented to a gourmet. Punctuality shows respect for the audience. The same goes for concert dress. articles.text: A Netflix series created by Ian Brennan and Ryan Murphy called Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story should be avoided by everyone with a pulse. The creators use mostly fabricated half truths and the “facts” used favor the sensational over reality. This season, the fourth in the Monster anthology true crime series, looks to explore misogyny, sexism, sexual identity, and how society has viewed women through the centuries. Watchers who want to explore those themes will be disappointed by the purposeful misrepresentation of all of the real-life people and how it harms the experiences of real people. Borden did not face many of the issues she is depicted as having in the show. Lizzie and her sister were paid $5,000, the equivalent of $173,000 in 2026, by their father for a property that they purchased from him for $1. Brennan uses Lizzie Borden as a stand-in for the issues women in high-society faced during Victorian era Massachusetts. Unlike in the show, Lizzie and her sister, Emma Borden, lived with their father and step-mother but both rarely ate dinner with their father and step-mother. Lizzie’s portrayal as a young helpless woman is far from her real life. She knew of her father’s wealth, properties, and was confident enough to take a trip to Europe two years before her father was murdered. Even when the film attempts to be historical Brennan cannot do it properly. Bridget Sullivan, the BorMonster: The Lizzie Borden Story trades truth for sensationalism. ®

Jim Kellogg noted that this would be “Chapter 2” of his tour of Old and New Architecture in the Piedmont City Center, following his July 8 walk, moving from 1907 to the 1930s and on to mid-century modern. When it is done well, he said, old and new mix together into a seamless part of Piedmont’s visual culture. The group started up Guilford Avenue, past the site of the Piedmont Art Gallery, which Frank C. Havens hired Julia Morgan to design in 1907. It closed after only 11 years, and the public tennis courts stand there today. The walk continued down Caperton Avenue, a beautiful, narrow street the group seldom walks, where Spanish Mission, Neo-Tudor, Piedmont Tradition and mid-century modern homes meld together. On Highland, the group stopped at 55 Hazel Lane, a rare Piedmont example of Hollywood Regency style, built in 1937. Jim described its bold, sleek lines, flat roofs and metal railings, almost like a 20th-century cruise ship with added theater and glamour. Like most Regency homes, it has a dramatic formal entry and a luxurious pool. Gloria Swanson, Joan Crawford and Douglas Fairbanks were among the stars who embraced the style. Next was 401 Wildwood Avenue, a 1964 mid-century modern masterwork and the only Piedmont house by Joe Esherick, who with William Wurster re-formed the UC Berkeley School of Architecture into the College of Environmental Design. Esherick is famous for The Sea Ranch, the Cannery at Fisherman’s Wharf and the Monterey Bay Aquarium, and for simple, understated designs with no Hollywood glamour. Next door, at 411 Wildwood, is a 1935 Monterey-style house. A revival of Spanish Mission with a romantic nod to the Old West, the style was made popular by stars such as Will Rogers, Clark Gable and Walt Disney. From 1991 to 2003 the house was home to KPIX journalist Wendy Tokuda, who, Mary Carter pointed out, was the daughter-in-law of Monty Hall of “Let’s Make a Deal” fame. Then came 431 Wildwood, a 6,500-square-foot “gothic revival” mansion designed by John Hudson Thomas and built in 1917, in the era when most of our city center went up. articles.text: David Mark Birnbaum, retired Deputy General Counsel at the University of California, passed away on September 25, 2026, in Piedmont, CA, from metastatic prostate cancer. He was 75 years old and had lived in Piedmont for 32 years. David was born in Passaic, New Jersey, to Jesse L. Birnbaum, long-time editor at Time magazine, and Elizabeth Haesly Birnbaum, a violist and music teacher. After growing up on Long Island, New York, David attended Colgate University for two years before moving to California to finish his undergraduate education at UC Santa Cruz, where he also learned to surf. David completed his education at UC Berkeley School of Law, obtaining his J.D. in 1976. That fall, he moved to Washington, DC, where he found employment as a staff attorney with The Review Panel on New Drug Regulation, a part of the (then) Department of Health, Education and Welfare. There he investigated allegations made by doctors at the Food and Drug Administration that the pharmaceutical industry had undue influence on the new drug approval process. After wrapping up that investigation, David went to work at the US Justice Department in the Civil Rights Division, prosecuting housing, education, and voting rights cases. In 1980, David returned to California, this time to Los Angeles where he worked for the law firm Gibson, Dunn and Crutcher for several years. In 1983, he moved back to the Bay Area to begin work in the Litigation Department of UC’s Office of General Counsel. For the next 30 years, David served in a variety of roles in the Office of General Counsel: Campus Counsel for UC Santa Cruz, Campus Counsel for UC Santa Barbara, and eventually, Deputy General Counsel. Even after retirement, David returned to UC to provide counsel to UCLA, during a period when that office in Los Angeles was understaffed. In 1984, David married Nancy Jean Marvel, a lawyer he met during his time in Washington, DC. After first settling in Oakland, they moved to Piedmont in 1994 where they raised their two daughters, Katie and Emily. David was an extremely active volunteer in his daughters’ school; he would often be the only dad driving on field trips. He also helped out in the classroom by advising on and editing students’ writing. He attended every David Birnbaum sports game his daughters played, as well as every school play, and every concert during their lengthy tenure with the Piedmont Children’s Choir. As a member of the Piedmont Community Church, David also taught Sunday School for many years when his daughters were young. After their retirement in 2013, David and Nancy spent a year living abroad in Aix-en-Provence, France, and Seville, Spain. They took advantage of their time there to see much of both countries, as well as Portugal and Morocco. Upon their return to the United States, David became involved in many volunteer activities, including Writer Coach Connection in Oakland, Berkeley Men’s Shelter, and Alameda County Food Bank. He joined the Board of Directors of Friends for Youth in Palo Alto, and served both as a deacon and as a member of the Board of Trustees for Piedmont Community Church. During the last part of David’s life, he and Nancy continued their travels around the world to China, India, Southeast Asia, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, the Amazon, Cuba, Tanzania, Peru, Brazil, Argentina, Mexico, and all over Europe. While traveling, David wrote extensively about these trips, publishing his observations and musings on Facebook. Once home, Nancy collected David’s writings along with accompanying photos, in a series of books, which now number eighty-four. David is survived by his wife Nancy, daughters Emily Birnbaum and Katie Stern, son-in-law Daniel Stern, grandsons Isaac and Elijah Stern, brother Nathan Birnbaum, and his beloved poodle Theo. A memorial service celebrating David’s life will be held at Piedmont Community Church, 400 Highland Avenue, on November 14, 2026, at 2:00 pm. In lieu of flowers, the family asks that tribute donations be made in David’s memory to the East Bay SPCA.

articles.text: One of the most common training conundrums is a dog who fears everyday objects. A sudden, forceful pull in the opposite direction because of a trash can can quickly take the joy out of a walk for any owner. Left unaddressed, these fears can persist or worsen, leading to an increasingly anxious dog and a frustrated owner. The good news is that, with patience, consistency, and plenty of positive reinforcement, you can help your dog become more confident. Let’s explore how to desensitize your dog to common everyday scares. Many of us have experienced the surprising, and sometimes painful, moment when our dog suddenly digs in their heels and refuses to pass an ordinary object. Common culprits include covered cars, as well as statues. Bring high-value treats and make sure your dog is securely fitted with a collar or harness to prevent them from running away. pages.text: Wednesday, October 21, 2026 21 Fear not, Fido: Desensitizing your dog to everyday objects By Sierra Berrick One of the most common training conundrums is a dog who fears everyday objects. A sudden, forceful pull in the opposite direction because of a trash can can quickly take the joy out of a walk for any owner. Left unaddressed, these fears can persist or worsen, leading to an increasingly anxious dog and a frustrated owner. The good news is that, with patience, consistency, and plenty of positive reinforcement, you can help your dog become more confident. Let’s explore how to desensitize your dog to common everyday scares. Many of us have experienced the surprising, and sometimes painful, moment when our dog suddenly digs in their heels and refuses to pass an ordinary object. Common culprits include covered cars, as well as statues. Bring high-value treats and make sure your dog is securely fitted with a collar or harness to prevent them from running away. Before approaching the “scary” object, begin walking back and forth at a swift pace, changing direction suddenly and often to encourage A collie is rewarded for her proximity to a previously scary golf cart. your dog to focus on you rather than the object. Reward for walking calmly by your side. Use a high, happy voice and avoid comforting the dog, as this can make their fear worse. Gradually work toward passing the object, rewarding often. The goal is to help your dog build a positive association with the object, not simply to get past it. Now let’s discuss moving or noisy items, such as vacuums or rolling carts. Start by introducing the item while it is turned off or stationary. Keep your dog on a leash, allowing enough room for them to retreat six feet. Begin tossing treats on the floor, creating a trail that encourages your dog to approach the object voluntarily. Use a cheerful tone and reward each step toward the object. If your dog backs away, give them space but only reward for forward progress; never drag the dog toward the “scary” item. As your dog becomes comfortable, continue rewarding them for standing near or sniffing the object. Once they are relaxed around the stationary item, repeat this process with the object turned on and/or moving. The key to overcoming everyday fears is patience, not pressure. Every dog progresses at a different pace, so celebrate small victories and keep training sessions short and positive. If your dog shows signs of intense fear or struggles to make progress, consider working with an experienced trainer. With time and trust, those once-terrifying trash cans, statues, and shiny floors can become just another part of the neighborhood. David Birnbaum dies on September 25 David Mark Birnbaum, retired Deputy General Counsel at the University of California, passed away on September 25, 2026, in Piedmont, CA, from metastatic prostate cancer. He was 75 years old and had lived in Piedmont for 32 years. David was born in Passaic, New Jersey, to Jesse L. Birnbaum, long-time editor at Time magazine, and Elizabeth Haesly Birnbaum, a violist and music teacher. After growing up on Long Island, New York, David attended Colgate University for two years before moving to California to finish his undergraduate education at UC Santa Cruz, where he also learned to surf. David completed his education at UC Berkeley School of Law, obtaining his J.D. in 1976. That fall, he moved to Washington, DC, where he found employment as a staff attorney with The Review Panel on New Drug Regulation, a part of the (then) Department of Health, Education and Welfare. There he investigated allegations made by doctors at the Food and Drug Administration that the pharmaceutical industry had undue influence on the new drug approval process. After wrapping up that investigation, David went to work at the US Justice Department in the Civil Rights Division, prosecuting housing, education, and voting rights cases. In 1980, David returned to California, this time to Los Angeles where he worked for the law firm Gibson, Dunn and Crutcher for several years. In 1983, he moved back to the Bay Area to begin work in the Litigation Department of UC’s Office of General Counsel. For the next 30 years, David served in a variety of roles in the Office of General Counsel: Campus Counsel for UC Santa Cruz, Campus Counsel for UC Santa Barbara, and eventually, Deputy General Counsel. Even after retirement, David returned to UC to provide counsel to UCLA, during a period when that office in Los Angeles was understaffed. In 1984, David married Nancy Jean Marvel, a lawyer he met during his time in Washington, DC. After first settling in Oakland, they moved to Piedmont in 1994 where they raised their two daughters, Katie and Emily. David was an extremely active volunteer in his daughters’ school; he would often be the only dad driving on field trips. He also helped out in the classroom by advising on and editing students’ writing. He attended every David Birnbaum sports game his daughters played, as well as every school play, and every concert during their lengthy tenure with the Piedmont Children’s Choir. As a member of the Piedmont Community Church, David also taught Sunday School for many years when his daughters were young. After their retirement in 2013, David and Nancy spent a year living abroad in Aix-en-Provence, France, and Seville, Spain. They took advantage of their time there to see much of both countries, as well as Portugal and Morocco. Upon their return to the United States, David became involved in many volunteer activities, including Writer Coach Connection in Oakland, Berkeley Men’s Shelter, and Alameda County Food Bank. He joined the Board of Directors of Friends for Youth in Palo Alto, and served both as a deacon and as a member of the Board of Trustees for Piedmont Community Church. During the last part of David’s life, he and Nancy continued their travels around the world to China, India, Southeast Asia, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, the Amazon, Cuba, Tanzania, Peru, Brazil, Argentina, Mexico, and all over Europe. While traveling, David wrote extensively about these trips, publishing his observations and musings on Facebook. Once home, Nancy collected David’s writings along with accompanying photos, in a series of books, which now number eighty-four. David is survived by his wife Nancy, daughters Emily Birnbaum and Katie Stern, son-in-law Daniel Stern, grandsons Isaac and Elijah Stern, brother Nathan Birnbaum, and his beloved poodle Theo. A memorial service celebrating David’s life will be held at Piedmont Community Church, 400 Highland Avenue, on November 14, 2026, at 2:00 pm. In lieu of flowers, the family asks that tribute donations be made in David’s memory to the East Bay SPCA.

articles.text: The Piedmont Seniors recently ventured to San Francisco to visit the American Conservatory Theater for its stage production of Alfred Hitchcock’s North by Northwest. Before the show began, the seniors had lunch at an upstairs venue at the theater, along with other senior groups visiting from the East Bay. After lunch, the group went to the theater for the show. Instead of recreating Hitchcock’s classic suspense film, this ACT version of North by Northwest is a fastpaced parody that has wildly inventive stagecraft, including using four mobile revolving doors and suitcases that unfold into miniature pop-up models to recreate iconic settings like the Plaza Hotel, the United Nations, and Mount Rushmore. This production also features mid-century music, jazzy dance numbers, and a breaking of the fourth wall. This production offers a dynamic seven-person cast and offers fast-paced physical comedy, dance, and acrobatics. Overall, it is a delightful, high-speed, and laugh-out-loud show that reimagines the 1959 Hitchcock classic with more of a childlike joy! After the curtain closed, several cast members came back on stage to address the audience and answer questions. All in all, as with all the Piedmont Seniors’ excursions, it was a very interesting day had by all! If you would like to find out more information about the Piedmont Seniors program, contact Janet Epstein, coordinator, at jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov. The Seniors meet monthly on Wednesday mornings from 10 a.m. to noon at the Piedmont Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue, Piedmont, in addition to going on monthly excursions throughout the Bay Area. articles.text: The phone rang one morning. My mom answered, and on the other end was her grandson, our son Chase. He was in trouble. He needed help, and he needed it now. It wasn’t Chase. To this day, my mom is certain it was him. The voice was his. It sounded exactly like him. That is what stays with me. Last year, Americans over 60 reported losing $7.7 billion to online criminals. That’s a 59% jump in one year, across more than 201,000 victims, with an average loss of $38,500. More than 12,000 people lost over $100,000 each. Federal researchers estimate that fewer than one in twenty victims ever reports the crime, so the real number is far higher. These are not careless people. They are our parents, our neighbors, our friends. More and more, they are us. So what changed? Artificial intelligence. The old “grandparent scam” relied on a muffled voice and a bad connection. Today a scammer needs only a few seconds of audio, pulled from a Facebook video or even a voicemail greeting, to clone the voice of someone you love. The call comes at 11 p.m. There’s been an accident. Don’t tell Mom and Dad. Please hurry. The FBI logged thousands of AI-related fraud complaints last year, with losses in the hundreds of millions. The technology is cheap, easy to find, and getting better every month. The four scams costing seniors the most • Investment fraud. This is now nearly half of all senior losses. It often starts with a friendly text “sent to the wrong number.” Over weeks or months, a friendship grows. Then comes an introduction to a trading platform showing incredible returns. The account balance is a screenshot. The money is gone. • Tech support scams. More than $1 billion lost last year. A pop-up or phone call claims to be Apple, Microsoft, or your bank and asks for remote access to your computer. • Romance scams. Built slowly and patiently on Facebook, Instagram, or dating apps. Then, suddenly, there’s an emergency. • Recovery scams. This one breaks my heart. Shortly after someone has been scammed, a “helper” reaches out promising to recover the money, and then takes whatever is left. A word from my world If you are buying or selling a home, wire fraud is very real. Criminals watch transaction emails and send fake wiring instructions days before closing. Never wire money based on an email. Pick up the phone, call your escrow officer at a number you already have, and confirm out loud. We tell every one of our clients this, and I will keep saying it. Six habits that protect us 1. Pause for ten minutes. Urgency is their weapon. Anything real can wait ten minutes. A scam can’t. 2. Hang up and call back on a number you already have, never the one they give you. 3. Choose a family code word. Something only your family knows. Ask for it before you send anything. 4. Never give anyone remote access to your computer, and never send cryptocurrency to someone you met online. No legitimate bank or agency will ask you to put cash into a crypto kiosk. 5. Talk to someone before you act. Scammers count on you feeling alone. Seniors who call a family member first are far less likely to lose money. 6. Always report it. File at ic3.gov or call the Justice Department’s Elder Fraud Hotline at 1-833-FRAUD-11. Being targeted by a professional criminal is nothing to be ashamed of. Please forward this to your parents, your children, your friends and your neighbors. Then pick up the phone and talk it through. That one conversation could protect someone you love. pages.text: Wednesday, October 21, 2026 23 Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. Dear MacMama, We are in our 80s. I have been a Mac user for decades and am comfortable (at this point) in the world of technology. But my wife is not at all, and I am starting to see some symptoms of dementia. She really wants a new iPhone, and I would love to get her one. All she really needs is the phone, messages and the camera. She does not need to get email on her phone. Is there a way to make it much simpler for her? P.L., Oakland Dear P.L., That’s a great question, and yes, Apple has some features that most people don’t know about to make the iPhone experience simpler for those who need an easier interface. Apple has a somewhat new feature (since September 2023 with iOS 17) called Assistive Access. This is a way to simplify the phone with a distraction-free interface. It can be set up with only the apps she will use, with large icons and text, and limited features. To set this up, make sure the phone is updated to the latest operating system. If you’re planning to get a new iPhone, if it’s not already at the latest, it will request that you update it when you start the phone setup. Once the phone is activated with your carrier and you have signed your wife into her Apple ID (or you make her a new one), you are ready to customize the phone into a much easier interface for her. Here are step-by-step directions. Go to Settings and choose Accessibility. Scroll all the way down until you see Assistive Access under General (in Accessibility). Choose that and then select Set Up Assistive Access, then Continue. Then you will confirm the Apple account of the primary user and press Continue. Then it will give you a list of apps that have been optimized for this feature with options that you can customize. The list of optimized apps is not long (you can still add other apps that have not been adapted for Assistive Access) and as you choose them, you will be given options. For example, when you choose Calls, you can choose whether the user can make and receive calls from contacts, favorites, or anyone. And you can decide whether voicemail is visible and choose to have both the keypad and the speaker available. Since your wife likes the camera, you can choose whether she can take photos only, or videos and photo and video selfies. With Messages you have similar options to the phone app, with an added feature of having messages read aloud by tapping. The other apps that have been adapted are Magnifier, Music, Photos and TV. When you have chosen all the apps that you want on the phone, scroll all the way to the bottom and select Continue. Then you will choose how you would like the icons to appear, either in rows or a grid. I find the grid to be easier for most people. After you choose this, you will be presented with a screen that informs you that to use emergency services or to exit Assistive Access you must triple-click the side button. If you have set up Face ID and a passcode, it will confirm that this has been set, but you will be guided to set up an Assistive Access passcode, which will allow you to turn this feature off. At this point, you can also set up a recovery Apple account, which I assume would be yours, in case she forgets her passcode. And then you will get instructions to exit Assistive Access. Finally, you will select the Start Using Assistive Access button. Of course, you can choose to keep the default iPhone interface, and just remove apps that she’s not using, but you can’t really remove the features that might be confusing, for example, on the camera. You can also, of course, make the text bigger and bold, increase the contrast, and make sure her most-used apps, like the phone, messages, and the camera, are in the dock. But with Assistive Access, your wife can have access to all of her photos, be able to call all of her friends and loved ones, and still take advantage of the excellent cameras on the newer iPhones. Cookie Segelstein is the MacMama, an Apple Certified Service Professional who provides Apple computer consultation and troubleshooting in your home and office. articles.text: Dear Editor of the Post: My name is Don Tamaki, and together with my wife, Suzie Ah-Tye, we have resided in Piedmont since 1993 and raised our twin sons in this community. It is with great pleasure to support Adam Hundt for City Council. We have enjoyed getting to know Adam as our neighbor, and found him to be informed, knowledgeable, curious, open-minded, approachable, and genuinely motivated to work diligently in the best interest of the community. The Council and Piedmont residents would benefit from Adam’s expertise in energy, climate policy, and wildfire mitigation. He has fresh ideas and perspectives to offer in these areas. We also had the opportunity to discuss with him matters of diversity and equity, and appreciated his responses. Finally, we note that he is the only candidate endorsed by the Alameda County Democratic Party. Adam Hundt has our vote. –Don Tamaki and Suzie Ah-Tye

articles.text: To the Editor: We are proud to endorse Bill Reichle for Piedmont City Council. Over nearly 30 years, we have developed enormous respect for his integrity, work ethic, and his ability to get things done for the communities he serves. Bill takes public service seriously but with humility. He does his homework, listens carefully, treats people with respect even when they disagree, stays after the meeting to reflect and forge consensus, and then delivers on his word. Those qualities are rarer than they should be in public life, but they are the hallmarks of our best public servants. Bill’s leadership at UC Berkeley prepared him ideally for the Piedmont City Council. He knows how to build a budget and to prioritize the things that have made Piedmont such a good place to live: strong schools, safe streets, community engagement, and good neighbors. Most of all, we trust Bill’s judgment, and know his character. If elected, he will work hard for every resident of Piedmont. We hope you’ll join us in voting to elect Bill. –Jeff and Becky Bleich
articles.title: Endorsing Bill Reichle

articles.text: Dear Piedmont Residents: I am writing to endorse Adam Hundt for Piedmont City Council in this election. I grew up in Piedmont in the 1990s and watched my father, a civil engineer and lawyer, participate in City Council meetings given his expertise. He wanted to help the community succeed and appreciated in this small-town environment there was an opportunity for him to engage directly with city government. I see in Adam qualities I respected in my father. Like my dad, Adam is eager to utilize his knowledge and expertise to address issues facing our city government. Given Piedmont’s numerous government functions — from city works to housing to parks and recreation — there is a need for someone with Adam’s curiosity and tenacity. Adam understands how to create public policies that are understandable, fair, and crafted to achieve specific strategic outcomes. He is honest, down to earth, and humble. When examining issues, he seeks out different opinions and perspectives. He may be new to Piedmont city government, but the city would benefit from having his perspective and problem-solving abilities on Council. I am excitedly supporting Adam for City Council and encourage other residents to do the same. Sincerely, –Katie Hendrickson
articles.title: Adam Hundt for City Council

Vote Required: 50%+1 Criteria: 1. Intent and structure of the tax (i.e., a % or rate for a sales or transfer tax, or a $ per parcel or square foot for a parcel tax). 2. Amount of tax generated per year and the duration of the tax. 3. Is this a Special or General tax? (The more specifically it’s described, the more easily one can figure out which it is, and the more credit they get.) 4. Where is the money specifically going? (particularly if a special tax). 5. Is there an existing or similar tax already in place? If so, that tax information should be included. SCORE: 4.5 Comments: The score was lowered from the maximum of five because it is misleading to say that the proceeds may go to the popular listed topics of parks, storm drains, police, fire, etc. This is a general tax, the proceeds of which can go to any city expense, and none may go to the listed recipients of the proceeds. The claim that the tax would remain until “ended by voters” is deceptive because it implies there is a mechanism within the measure allowing for a public opportunity to terminate the tax. Instead, there is no probable way to end this tax other than the difficult citizen initiative process. Effectively, this tax would probably be permanent.
